implementation_notes: C++11 supplies the dispatch primitive but not the composite: launch one std::async(std::launch::async, ...) per part, keep the futures in a vector ordered by part index (that vector is the correlation state), then get() each future and merge as results become available - or in index order when the merge is not commutative. The routing decision is a registry or function-pointer lookup in the split loop; the aggregation is a fold over the resolved values. Bound the fan-out with your own task queue once part counts grow, since one thread per part stops paying off quickly; the flow-graph variant is the next step up.
pitfalls: std::async's default policy is std::launch::async | std::launch::deferred: omitting std::launch::async lets the runtime defer parts to the caller thread and silently serialises the pipeline.
Destroying an unfinished std::future from std::async blocks in the shared state's destructor; dropping the vector without get() turns the aggregate barrier into a hidden join.
One thread per part does not scale: for hundreds of parts the spawn cost dominates the element-processing time.

variants.name: oneTBB flow graph (fan-out nodes, join/aggregation sink)
variants.idiom_name: tbb::flow::graph with function_node per part kind + join/limiter nodes
variants.implementation_notes: oneTBB's flow graph is the library-grade form: the splitter is a broadcast_node (or a function_node emitting many messages), each part kind gets a function_node with its own concurrency, the graph edges encode the routing table, and a join_node or an aggregation sink with graph::wait_for_all() performs the completion barrier. Choose it when routing really is a graph - per-kind concurrency limits, continuous part streams, back-pressure via limiter_node - rather than one batch that is folded once.
pitfalls: A node without a limiter_node, buffer_node or explicit concurrency argument accepts unbounded parallel work; bound it or one large composite saturates the arena.
Nodes and edges must be destroyed in the documented order and after wait_for_all(); deleting nodes while messages are in flight is undefined.
